article.overview:
A wide-angle camera is an imager whose lens records a much larger field of view than a standard or narrow-angle lens. From a fixed altitude, a wider field gives a wider swath and more ground per frame, but each detector pixel covers more ground, so the ground scale is coarser. The term describes optical geometry. It does not describe one design, one detector or one spectral band, so it covers instruments that differ in age, mission and recording method.

Scope of this article. The article uses 'wide-angle' where a source describes a camera's field as wide. Two flown lunar examples are described. (1) The LRO Wide Angle Camera (WAC), part of the LROC instrument pair on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter; its own source calls it a Wide Angle Camera [1][2]. It is a seven-band push-frame imager with a monochrome mode. (2) The Apollo 15 Metric (Mapping) Camera, a film frame camera in the command and service module (CSM) Scientific Instrument Module (SIM) bay, with a 74 by 74 degree field [4]. The source calls it a mapping camera and does not use the term wide-angle; it is included here as a wide-field example, and that classification is this article's choice.

Status. The LRO WAC is described by its sources as flown on LRO [1][2][3]. The Apollo 15 metric camera is described as flown on Apollo 15 [4]. No flight-qualified-but-unflown or proposed wide-angle lunar camera was verified in this run, so none is described. A 1966 Lunar Orbiter wide-angle lens was identified by search, but its scanned source could not be read, so it is mentioned only as an unverified lead.

Boundaries and cross-references. High-resolution and narrow-angle imaging is in 027 (High-resolution camera) and 045 (Narrow-angle camera); the LRO narrow-angle cameras are the high-resolution partners of the WAC. Strip-scanning and mast-mounted panoramic imaging is in 026 (Panoramic camera). Stereo and terrain-model products are in 028 (Terrain mapping camera) and 029 (Stereo camera); photogrammetric mapping is in 049 (Photogrammetry system). Single broad-band imaging is in 043 (Panchromatic camera), which discusses the WAC monochrome mode. Multi-band spectral imaging is in 034 (Multispectral imager); the WAC seven-band set is described here only as far as its wide-field design needs. Visible-light imaging is in 039 (Visible-light camera).
article.description:
A wide-angle lens records a large angular field in one frame or one scan. On an orbiter, a wide field means a wide ground swath, so one orbit can produce a broad, consistent mosaic. The trade-off is ground resolution: the same detector pixel covers more ground at the edges of the field than at the centre, and the image is more distorted.

The LRO WAC is a digital camera. Its design uses two short-focal-length lenses, one for the visible bands and one for the ultraviolet bands. Both lenses image onto the same 1024 by 1024 pixel CCD. A prism lets both optical paths share the detector, and seven narrow-band interference filters are bonded to the detector surface [1].

The Apollo 15 Metric (Mapping) Camera is a film camera. It used a 76 mm (3 in) lens and recorded 114 mm square frames on 127 mm (5 in) black-and-white aerial film. The camera was one part of a mapping system with a laser altimeter and a stellar camera [4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
Global morphology basemap (WAC). The WAC was designed to provide global imaging at 100 m/pixel in seven colour bands. In monochrome mode it was to be run as a single-band global basemap, with a morphologic basemap taken at incidence angles of 60 to 80 degrees [1]. These are design intentions in the instrument paper, not a report of achieved coverage.

Multispectral mineral context (WAC). The two UV filters (320 and 360 nm) were selected to be sensitive to ilmenite-bearing material, which has a distinct absorption near 450 to 500 nm. The visible filters were selected to be sensitive to changes in the magnesium number of olivine [1].

Polar illumination and permanently shadowed regions (WAC). The paper describes a monochrome swath of about 104 km from the nominal 50 km orbit, giving repeat coverage each orbit near the poles. It describes a planned year-long illumination time-lapse of the poles, and a planned mapping of permanently shadowed and sunlit terrain at both poles at about 100 m scale [1]. These are the paper's planned products; the article does not report them as completed results.

Metric mapping and geodetic control (Apollo 15). The Apollo metric camera was designed to obtain precise metric photographs, together with time-correlated star photography, for selenodetic reference and cartographic control. Its stated objectives included photomapping at scales up to 1:250,000 and synoptic geological imagery at about 20 m ground resolution [4]. The source also says the camera supplied supporting photography for the SIM panoramic camera and other CSM experiments [4].
article.operating_principle:
LRO WAC (push-frame imaging). In colour mode, each of the seven filters covers its own strip of the detector. Repeated imaging gives overlapping framelets, so each colour band has continuous coverage on the ground. The visible lens is a 6.0 mm focal length, f/5.5 design with a 90 degree field across 1008 detector pixels. The UV lens is a 4.7 mm focal length, f/5.1 design with a 60 degree field across 512 detector pixels. UV data are acquired by summing 4 by 4 pixel blocks because UV signal is low. The UV light reaches the detector through a periscope-type path inside the prism [1].

The WAC electronics digitise each pixel to 12 bits. Correlated double sampling gives a net 11-bit range, which is companded to 8 bits and compressed before downlink [1]. In monochrome mode the camera records a single band, nominally 605 nm, over the full detector width [1][2].

Apollo 15 Metric Camera (film frame). A pair of continuously rotating disks with a capping blade formed the shutter. Seven exposure times between 0.004 and 0.067 seconds were available. The film was held flat during exposure by a glass stage plate with 112 reseau crosses. Eight fiducial marks, just outside the image format, defined the optical axis on each frame. The film plate moved in the direction of flight during exposure to compensate for forward motion [4].
article.scientific_importance:
The LRO WAC matters because it supplies the broad, consistent context that narrow-angle images do not. Its design combines a global visible basemap with ultraviolet and visible spectral filters, so one instrument supports both morphology and composition work [1]. The LROC instrument paper presents the WAC as the global imaging camera of the LROC pair, with the two Narrow Angle Cameras providing the high-resolution images [1]. The NASA Photojournal mosaic shows a WAC-based global view of the Moon [5].

The Apollo 15 metric camera is significant as a flown example of a dedicated photogrammetric mapping camera from lunar orbit. The source reports 3375 frames taken, some over unlit terrain in support of the laser altimeter [4]. Its precision and its use for surface mapping are described in the source as objectives. The accessed source does not report an independent accuracy assessment.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a wide-angle camera. The examples below differ in recording method (digital push-frame versus film), mission and purpose. The two examples are not directly comparable, so no comparison table is given. Each value is tied to a named instrument and source. A value that the accessed sources do not state is recorded as 'not publicly specified'.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are not publicly specified for either example in the accessed sources. The LRO WAC is described with a 1024 by 1024 detector and 6.0 mm and 4.7 mm lenses (specifications page), but no physical envelope is given. The Apollo 15 camera's 114 mm by 114 mm image format and 76 mm focal length are image and optical dimensions, not instrument dimensions.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: LRO WAC: 0.9 kg (LROC specifications page; not checked against the instrument paper). Apollo 15 Metric Camera: not publicly specified in the accessed PDS document.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LRO WAC: peak 2.7 W and average 2.6 W (LROC specifications page). Operates from the 28 V spacecraft bus on a separately switched circuit (Robinson 2010, spacecraft interface discussion). Apollo 15 Metric Camera: not publicly specified in the accessed PDS document; the camera was controlled from the command module, with heater and camera functions switched by the crew.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
For the LRO WAC, the instrument paper describes real-time telemetry monitoring of voltage and temperature during S-band contacts, trend analysis of stored telemetry during Ka-band contacts, and health monitoring from dark-pixel statistics in acquired images [1]. The WAC electronics are powered from the spacecraft 28 V bus on a separately switched circuit [1]. Daily command loads are generated for the WAC and the NACs [1]. The WAC frame buffer is double-buffered in the Sequence and Compressor System so that WAC and NAC data can share one spacecraft interface [1].

For the Apollo 15 metric camera, the crew could turn the camera heaters and camera functions on and off from the command module. The controls included image motion compensation and the camera's velocity-to-height setting, and the camera system could be extended or retracted on its rails [4]. The film container was recovered by EVA during trans-Earth coast [4].

Thermal, radiation and dust requirements for either camera are not described in the accessed sources, beyond the telemetry and protective-cover statements above.
article.limitations:
Distortion. The WAC wide field produces more distortion than the Narrow Angle Cameras, so the calibration needs an additional distortion term [1].

Sensitivity and linearity. The detector fill factor is 20 percent, lowering quantum efficiency. The WAC optics are described as fast enough to compensate [1]. The paper reports a linear response between 5 and 90 percent of saturation, and a non-linear response above about 1800 DN after background correction [1].

Resolution. The WAC ground scale (about 75 m/pixel from 50 km) is coarser than the NAC scale. Fine morphology needs other instruments, as noted in the cross-references.

Spectral coverage. The WAC has seven bands and a monochrome mode. It does not provide continuous spectra.

Apollo film. The Apollo 15 metric camera recorded film. Its data were not available in real time, because the film container was recovered by EVA [4].

Classification. The Apollo metric camera wide field is a classification made by this article; the source calls it a mapping camera.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The LRO WAC is an orbiter payload on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. The relevant stages are spacecraft integration, launch, lunar transfer, orbit insertion and commissioning. LRO launch date is given as 18 June 2009 [3]. The instrument paper states that WAC calibration images were to be obtained during the cruise phase [1]. The paper nominal orbit for WAC monochrome imaging is 50 km [1]. Integration interfaces named in the sources are the 28 V spacecraft bus and the SCS data interface [1]. The Apollo 15 metric camera was an orbiter payload in the CSM SIM bay, carried on structural shelves and not deployed to the surface [4].
transportation_process: Integrate the WAC optics, prism, filter assembly, detector and electronics into the Sequence and Compressor System interface on the LRO spacecraft (Robinson 2010, Sections 3.2 and 3.3).
Launch LRO (18 June 2009) and perform lunar transfer and orbit insertion [3].
Complete cruise-phase WAC calibration imaging as planned in the instrument paper [1].
Operate the WAC in monochrome mode from the nominal 50 km orbit for basemap imaging, and in multispectral mode for colour products [1].

For the Apollo 15 metric camera, the camera system was integrated into the SIM bay mapping unit with the laser altimeter and stellar camera, deployed on rails for operation, and the film container was recovered by the Command Module Pilot during EVA on trans-Earth coast [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The LRO WAC is not deployed. It is a fixed orbiter instrument. The Apollo 15 metric camera was mounted on a rail-type mechanism in the SIM bay and extended for operation so that the stellar camera had an unobstructed field of view [4].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Orbiter examples: LRO WAC (LRO, 2009 launch) [1][3]; Apollo 15 Metric (Mapping) Camera (CSM SIM bay, Apollo 15) [4]. An unverified Lunar Orbiter wide-angle lens lead is noted in historical_significance.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted for either example. Such a claim would need verified interface documents for the named vehicle. The accessed sources describe no lander or rover interface for either camera.

article.historical_significance:
The Apollo 15 metric camera was part of the lunar orbital mapping system carried in the Apollo 15 SIM bay. The source reports 3375 frames taken for metric mapping and geodetic control [4]. The accessed source does not place it in a wider sequence of Apollo missions.

The LRO WAC is part of the LROC pair on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. The LROC instrument paper documents its design, calibration and planned products [1]. NASA Photojournal presents a WAC-based global view of the Moon as a public image product [5]. The WAC seven-band global dataset was intended to complement earlier multispectral datasets from Clementine, Kaguya (SELENE) and Chandrayaan-1 [1].

A Lunar Orbiter wide-angle lens was identified in a search of the NASA technical report archive [6]. The scanned PDF could not be read in this run, so the article does not use any value from it. It is noted only as an unverified lead for later research.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- WAC field of view and focal length. The LROC specifications page and the instrument paper give different field values (92, 61 and 59 degrees versus 90 and 60 degrees) [1][2]. Both are recorded. The specifications page is dated 2013 by its footnote [2]. Resolve from instrument calibration documents before using either value in a calculation.
- UV ground sample distance. The paper gives 384 m/pixel [1]; the specifications page gives 385 m/pixel for 4x4 binned UV [2]. Not resolved here.
- Design versus as-built filters. Paper band names are design values; as-built centres are taken from the specifications page [1][2].
- Orbit history. The 50 km orbit is the paper nominal design value [1]. LRO actual orbit history for the WAC is not established here.
- WAC operating status. NASA lists LRO as an active mission at the time of research [3]; no instrument-level status was verified.
- WAC mass and power. From the specifications page [2]; not checked against a second source.
- WAC hardware photograph. Credit, date and flight or engineering status are not stated on the page [2]. Reuse rights not verified.
- Apollo 15 metric camera. Mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the PDS document [4]. The related 1971 Fairchild technical report was not read. A search summary gave lens and stellar-camera figures that differ from the PDS document; those figures are not used.
- Apollo 15 metric camera classification. The source does not call it wide-angle; its inclusion is an article classification.
- Lunar Orbiter. A wide-angle lens was identified by search but not verified; no value from it is used.
- Image and mosaic rights. NASA and LROC images were checked for HTTP 200 and image type, but NASA and LROC reuse terms were not checked. No public-domain status is asserted.
- Lunar landing sites. This article does not recommend lunar landing sites or locations. That is deferred by the user.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Both registry images were verified to return HTTP 200 (image/jpeg) without query strings. The PIA13516 image appears in payload.article.overview_images, which is shown in the Markdown article overview. The LRO WAC hardware photograph appears in physical_specifications.examples[0].images, which is shown in the Markdown article within Example 1. No image is placed in the Apollo 15 metric camera example because no direct asset was verified. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so that each section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master registry.

data_quality_notes: WAC field of view: the LROC specifications page gives 92 (monochrome), 61 (visible) and 59 (UV) degrees; the LRO instrument paper (Robinson et al. 2010, Section 3.2.1) gives 90 degrees for the visible lens over 1008 pixels and 60 degrees for the UV lens over 512 pixels. Both recorded; not averaged. The specifications page is footnoted 'At an altitude of 50 km' and was last updated 8 May 2013. The discrepancy should be resolved from calibration documents. Note for the orchestrator: payload 043 cites the specifications-page values; it may need reconciliation with the paper. Not edited here.
WAC UV ground sample distance: 384 m/pixel (paper, Section 3.2) versus 385 m/pixel for 4x4 binned UV (specifications page). Not resolved; difference is small.

WAC filters: design band names in the paper (320, 360, 415, 565, 605, 645, 690 nm) differ from the as-built centres on the specifications page (321, 360, 415, 566, 604, 643, 689 nm). As-built centres used. FWHM values extracted from Table 4 for five bands only; 643 and 689 nm FWHM not extracted.
WAC mass and power (0.9 kg; 2.7 W peak; 2.6 W average) come from the specifications page only. Not checked against the instrument paper, and the page is dated 2013.
WAC orbit: the 50 km orbit is the paper's nominal design value for monochrome imaging. LRO's actual orbit history for the WAC was not established in this run.

WAC operating status: NASA's LRO page lists the mission as an active mission at the time of reading. No instrument-level status for the WAC was verified. The page does not give launch vehicle or orbit.

WAC planned products (illumination time-lapse at the poles; 100 m/pixel global basemap; permanently shadowed region mapping) are design intentions stated in the instrument paper. They are not reported as completed results in this article.

WAC hardware photograph (LROC specifications page, alt text 'LROC Wide Angle Camera hardware'): no caption, credit or date on the page; flight-unit or engineering-model status not stated. Reuse rights not verified. Included because the direct asset returned HTTP 200 and is on the LROC page.

Apollo 15 Metric (Mapping) Camera: the PDS instrument overview gives the 76 mm lens, 74 by 74 degree field, 166 km square coverage from 110 km, 114 mm image size, 127 mm film, 457.2 m film capacity (3500 frames) and 3375 frames taken. Mass, power and dimensions are not stated. The source describes it as a mapping camera; the wide-field classification is this article's choice.

Apollo 15 Metric Camera: a search summary gave a 76 mm stellar-camera lens and a Fairchild 1971 technical report was cited. Neither was read, and no value from them is used. The stellar camera in the PDS document uses a 35 mm lens.
Apollo 15 Metric Camera image: the PDS document figures (Figures 1 and 2 from Cameron et al. 1972) were not extracted; no direct image asset was verified. No image is included for this example.

Lunar Orbiter wide-angle lens: identified by search in the NASA Technical Reports Server (record 19660009057). The scanned PDF could not be read because no OCR tool was available in this run. A search summary gave an 80 mm focal length for the wide-angle lens and a 31.6 by 37.4 km image at 46 km; these values are unverified and are not used.

Image coverage: two registry images (NASA PIA13516 mosaic and the LROC WAC hardware photograph) were verified to return HTTP 200. The NASA image has a credit line; the hardware photograph has no credit. Full-resolution downloads were not checked.
Image reuse rights: neither NASA nor LROC reuse terms were checked for these images. No public-domain status is asserted.
No lunar landing-site or location recommendations are made. No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted for either example.

PolCam (Danuri/KPLO) was considered as a possible wide-angle polarimetric camera. A search summary described its field as about 10 degrees, so it was not classified as wide-angle, and no primary source for it was read in this run. It is not described in this article.
